title: Unseen stewards and demon executioners
source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτα ὁ Κέλσος τὸ ὁμολογουμένως ὑπὸ Χριστιανῶν καὶ Ἰουδαίων λεγόμενον τίθησιν, ἀπολογουμένων περὶ τῆς τῶν εἰδωλοθύτων ἀποχῆς καὶ φασκόντων μὴ δεῖν συνεστιᾶσθαι δαίμοσι τοὺς ἀνακειμένους τῷ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεῷ· πρὸς ὃ εἶπε τὰ ἐκκείμενα. ἡμεῖς μὲν οὖν, ὅσον ἐπὶ βρώμασι καὶ πόμασι, τοῦ συνεστιᾶσθαι δαίμοσι τρόπους ἄλλους οὐκ ἴσμεν ἢ καθ᾿ οὓς τὰ καλούμενα παρὰ τοῖς πολλοῖς ἱερόθυτα ἐσθίει τις καὶ πίνει τὸν τῶν παρὰ τοῖς δαιμονίοις γινομένων σπονδῶν οἶνον· ὁ δὲ Κέλσος οἴεται συνεστιᾶσθαι δαίμοσι καὶ τὸν σίτου μεταλαμβάνοντα καὶ ὅπως ποτ᾿ οὖν οἴνου πίνοντα καὶ ἀκροδρύων γευόμενον, ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰ μόνου ὕδατός τις μεταλαμβάνει, καὶ ἐν τούτῳ φησὶ συνεστιᾶσθαι δαίμοσι τὸν πίνοντα. προστίθησι δὲ τούτοις ὅτι καὶ ὁ τὸν ἀέρα τοῦτον ἀναπνέων παρὰ δαιμόνων τινῶν καὶ τοῦτον λαμβάνει, χαριζομένων δαιμόνων τῶν ἐπὶ τοῦ ἀέρος προστεταγμένων τὸν τῆς ἀναπνοῆς τοῖς ζῴοις ἀέρα. ὁ βουλόμενος τοίνυν παραστησάτω τῷ Κέλσου λόγῳ καὶ δεικνύτω, πῶς οὐ θεῖοί τινες ἄγγελοι θεοῦ ἀλλὰ δαίμονες, ὧν ὅλον τὸ γένος ἐστὶ φαῦλον, προστεταγμένοι εἰσὶ πάντα τὰ προειρημένα οἰκονομεῖν. καὶ ἡμεῖς μὲν γάρ φαμεν οὐ χωρὶς προστασίας ἀοράτων, ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω, γεωργῶν καὶ ἄλλων οἰκονόμων οὐ μόνον τῶν ἀπὸ γῆς φυομένων ἀλλὰ καὶ παντὸς ναματιαίου ὕδατος καὶ ἀέρος τὴν γῆν φέρειν τὰ ὑπὸ φύσεως λεγόμενα διοικεῖσθαι, καὶ τὸ ὕδωρ ἐν ταῖς πηγαῖς καὶ τοῖς αὐθιγενέσι ποταμοῖς ὀμβρεῖν καὶ φέρεσθαι, καὶ τὸν ἀέρα ἀδιάφθορον τηρεῖσθαι καὶ ζωτικὸν τοῖς ἀναπνέουσιν αὐτὸν γίνεσθαι. οὐ μὴν τοὺς ἀοράτους φαμὲν εἶναι δαίμονας· ἀλλ᾿. εἰ χρὴ ἀποτολμήσαντα λέγειν τινὰ. εἴπερ ταῦτα δαιμόνων ἐστὶν ἔργα. φήσομεν ὅτι λιμοὶ καὶ ἀφορίαι σταφυλῆς καὶ ἀκροδρύων καὶ αὐχμοὶ ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ τοῦ ἀέρος διαφθορὰ ἐπὶ λύμῃ τῶν καρπῶν ἔσθ᾿ ὅτε δὲ καὶ τῷ τῶν ζῴων θανάτῳ καὶ τῷ κατὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων λοιμῷ. πάντα ταῦτα δαίμονες αὐτουργοῦσι δήμιοι, κρίσει τινὶ θείᾳ λαβόντες ἐξουσίαν ἐν καιροῖς τισι ταῦτ᾿ ἐνεργεῖν εἴτε εἰς ἐπιστροφὴν ἀνθρώπων, ἐπὶ τὴν χύσιν τῆς κακίας ἐξοκειλάντων, εἴτε καὶ εἰς γυμνάσιον τοῦ λογικοῦ γένους· ἵν᾿ οἱ μὲν καὶ ἐν τοῖς τοσούτοις εὐσεβεῖς μένοντες καὶ μηδαμῶς χείρους γινόμενοι φανεροὶ τέως τοῖς μὴ βλέπουσιν αὐτῶν τὴν ἕξιν ἀοράτοις καὶ ὁρατοῖς θεαταῖς γένωνται, οἱ δ᾿ ἐναντίως μὲν διακείμενοι κλέπτοντες δὲ τὴν τῆς κακίας ἐπίδειξιν ἐλεγχθέντες ὑπὸ τῶν συμβαινόντων ὁποῖοί εἰσιν αὐτοί τε ἑαυτῶν συναισθηθῶσι καὶ δῆλοι τοῖς. ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω. θεαταῖς γένωνται.
pass_a_gloss: After these Celsus sets down (τίθημι) the thing said by agreement (ὁμολογουμένως) by Christians and Jews, defending themselves (ἀπολογέομαι) about the abstention from things sacrificed to idols and asserting (φάσκω) that those dedicated (ἀνάκειμαι) to the God over all (ὁ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεός) must not feast together with demons; to which he said the things set out. We then, so far as concerns foods and drinks (πόματα), know no other ways (τρόποι) of feasting with demons than those according to which someone eats the things called by the many sacred offerings (ἱερόθυτα) and drinks the wine of the libations (σπονδαί) made among the demons (δαιμόνια). But Celsus thinks that he too feasts with demons who partakes of bread (σῖτος) and drinks wine in whatever way and tastes fruits (ἀκρόδρυα), but also if someone partakes of water alone, in this too he says the drinker feasts with demons. And he adds to these that also he who breathes (ἀναπνέω) this air (ἀήρ) receives this too from certain demons, the demons appointed (προστάσσω) over the air granting (χαρίζομαι) the air of breathing (ἀναπνοή) to living creatures. Let him who wishes then stand beside (παρίστημι) Celsus's argument (λόγος) and show how not certain divine angels (ἄγγελοι) of God but demons, whose whole race (γένος) is base (φαῦλος), are appointed to manage (οἰκονομέω) all the things aforesaid. For we too say that not without the oversight (προστασία) of invisible (ἀόρατοι), so to name, farmers (γεωργοί) and other stewards (οἰκονόμοι) not only of things growing (φύω) from earth but also of every flowing (ναματιαῖος) water and air does the earth bear the things said to be governed (διοικέω) by nature (φύσις), and the water in the springs (πηγαί) and the self-sprung (αὐθιγενής) rivers pour (ὀμβρέω) and be carried, and the air be kept (τηρέω) uncorrupted (ἀδιάφθορος) and become life-giving (ζωτικός) to those breathing it. Not however do we say the invisible ones are demons; but, if one must, venturing (ἀποτολμάω), say something, if indeed these are works of demons, we shall say that famines (λιμοί) and barrenness (ἀφορία) of grape-vine (σταφυλή) and of fruit trees and droughts (αὐχμοί), but also the corruption (διαφθορά) of the air for ruin (λύμη) of the crops (καρποί), and at times also for the death of animals and for the pestilence (λοιμός) against men, all these demons work themselves (αὐτουργέω) as executioners (δήμιοι), having received authority (ἐξουσία) by some divine judgment (κρίσις θεία) at certain times (καιροί) to effect (ἐνεργέω) these, either for the conversion (ἐπιστροφή) of men who have run aground (ἐξοκέλλω) onto the outpouring (χύσις) of wickedness, or also for the exercise/training (γυμνάσιον) of the rational race (λογικὸν γένος); so that some, even in such things remaining pious (εὐσεβής) and in no way becoming worse, may become manifest (φανερός) to the invisible and visible spectators (θεαταί) not till then (τέως) seeing their state (ἕξις), and the others, disposed (διάκειμαι) the opposite way but stealing (κλέπτω) [i.e. concealing] the display (ἐπίδειξις) of wickedness, being refuted/exposed (ἐλέγχω) by the events (τὰ συμβαίνοντα) as to what sort they are, may both perceive (συναισθάνομαι) themselves and become evident (δῆλοι) to the, so to name, spectators.
pass_b_english: After this, Celsus sets down what Christians and Jews alike say when they defend their abstaining from things offered to idols and declare that those who are devoted to the God over all must not feast with demons. It was in answer to this that he said what has been quoted. So far as foods and drinks are concerned, we know no other ways of feasting with demons than these: when someone eats what most people call sacred offerings, and drinks the wine of the libations poured to demons. But Celsus thinks that even the man who eats bread, and drinks wine in any way at all, and tastes fruits, feasts with demons. Indeed, even if someone takes only water, he says that in this too the drinker feasts with demons. And to this he adds that the man who breathes this air also receives it from certain demons, since the demons set over the air grant living creatures the air they breathe.

Let anyone who wishes, then, take the side of Celsus’s argument, and show how it is not certain divine angels of God, but demons, whose whole race is evil, who have been appointed to manage all the things just mentioned. For we too say that it is not without the oversight of invisible farmers, if I may call them so, and of other stewards, not only of what grows from the earth but also of all flowing water and of the air, that the earth brings forth what is said to be governed by nature, that water pours forth and runs in springs and in rivers that rise of themselves, and that the air is kept uncorrupted and becomes life-giving to those who breathe it.

Yet we do not say that these invisible beings are demons. But if one must venture to say something, and if these things really are the work of demons, we shall say this: famines, failures of the vine and of fruit trees, droughts, and also the corruption of the air to the ruin of crops, and sometimes even to the death of animals and to plague among men, all these the demons bring about with their own hands, as executioners. They have received authority by a certain divine judgment to work these things at certain times, either for the conversion of men who have been carried away into the flood of wickedness, or else for the training of the rational race.

This happens so that those who remain pious even amid such great calamities, and in no way become worse, may become manifest to the spectators, invisible and visible, who until then did not see their true state; while those who are disposed the opposite way but hide the display of their wickedness, being shown up by events for what they are, may become aware of themselves and may become plain to the spectators, if I may call them so.

choices.choice: Origen restates Celsus’s words from 8.28 in his own phrasing here; since this is a paraphrase, not a fresh quotation, I did not put it in quotation marks. ‘Sacred offerings’ renders ἱερόθυτα, the word used in 1 Corinthians 10:28 (uncited inline: it is a common term, not a clear allusion). ὀμβρεῖν (literally ‘to rain’) is rendered ‘pours forth’ of water in springs. ‘Rivers that rise of themselves’ renders αὐθιγενέσι ποταμοῖς (spring-fed, native rivers). The clause ‘εἴπερ ταῦτα δαιμόνων ἐστὶν ἔργα’ is taken as a cautious condition looking ahead to the list of disasters. ἐξοκέλλω (‘run aground’, and so ‘be carried away’) with χύσις (‘outpouring, flood’) is rendered ‘carried away into the flood of wickedness’, avoiding the mixed image of running aground in a flood. ‘Calamities’ renders τοῖς τοσούτοις (‘such great things’), which points back to the disasters just listed. The ‘spectators, invisible and visible’ may echo 1 Corinthians 4:9 (‘a spectacle to the world, to angels and to men’); this is only possible, so it is not cited inline.
